(p-168) Surat al-Tin

There are two opinions concerning it:

The first: it is Meccan. This is the view of the majority, including al-Hasan and ʿAṭāʾ.

The second: it is Madani. This was related by al-Mawardi from Ibn ʿAbbas and Qatadah.

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿By the fig and the olive﴾. Concerning these two there are seven opinions.

The first: it refers to the well-known fig and the well-known olive. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Hasan, ʿAṭāʾ, Mujahid, ʿIkrimah, Jabir ibn Zayd, and Ibrahim. Some exegetes mentioned (p-169) that He swore by the fig because it is a fruit free from any impurity of distress, and this indicates the power of the One who made it upon that quality. Each single fig was made to be the size of a morsel. He swore by the olive because of the great benefit derived from it.

The second: the fig is the Mosque of Noah, peace be upon him, which was built upon al-Judi. The olive is Bayt al-Maqdis. ʿAṭiyyah related this from Ibn ʿAbbas.

The third: the fig is the Masjid al-Haram, and the olive is al-Masjid al-Aqsa. This was said by al-Dahhak.

The fourth: the fig is the Mosque of Damascus, and the olive is Bayt al-Maqdis. This was said by Kaʿb, Qatadah, and Ibn Zayd.

The fifth: they are two mountains. This was said by ʿIkrimah in one narration. It was related from Qatadah that he said: the fig is the mountain upon which Damascus stands, and the olive is the mountain upon which Bayt al-Maqdis stands.

The sixth: the fig is the Mosque of the People of the Cave, and the olive is the Mosque of Iliya. This was said by al-Qurazi.

The seventh: the fig is mountains between Hulwan and Hamadhan, and the olive is mountains in al-Sham. This was related by al-Farra'.

As for "Tur Sinin": Tur is a mountain. Concerning it there are two opinions.

(p-170) The first: it is the mountain upon which Allah spoke to Musa, peace be upon him. This was said by Kaʿb al-Ahbar, and most scholars agree.

The second: it is a mountain in al-Sham. This was said by Qatadah.

As for "Sinin": it is a dialectal form of Sina'. ʿAli, Saʿd ibn Abi Waqqas, Abu al-ʿAliyah, and Abu Mijlaz read "Wa-Tur Sina'" with a long vowel and a hamzah, with the sin vowelled with a fatha. Ibn Mas'ud, Abu al-Darda', and Abu Haywah read "Wa-Tur Sina'" like them, except that they vowelled the sin with a kasra. Abu Raja' and al-Jahdari read "Sinin" as it is in the Mushaf, but they vowelled the sin with a fatha. Ibn al-Anbari said: "Sinin" is Sina'.

They differed about its meaning. It was said: its meaning is "the good." It was said: "the blessed." It was said: it is a name for the tree around it. We have explained this in Surat al-Mu'minun [23:20]. Al-Zajjaj said: it has been read here as "Wa-Tur Sina'," and this is more fitting given His statement, exalted is He: ﴿and a tree that grows out of Mount Sinai﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 20]. Muqatil said: every mountain in which there is fruit-bearing trees is "Sinin," and Sina' is the language of the Nabat.

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿and this secure city﴾ means Makkah, where the one who fears is secure in the Jahiliyyah (p-171) and in Islam. Al-Farra' said: the meaning of "al-Amin" is "the secure," and the Arabs say of the trustworthy: "amin" (secure).

The poet said:

Do you not know, O Asma, woe to you, that I have sworn an oath not to betray my trustworthy one?

He means "amini" (my secure one).

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Certainly We created man﴾ is the answer to the oath. Concerning the intended meaning of "man" here there are five opinions.

The first: he is Kaladah ibn Usayd. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah. This was said by ʿAṭāʾ.

The third: Abu Jahl ibn Hisham.

The fourth: ʿUtbah and Shaybah; al-Mawardi related both.

(p-172) The fifth: it is a generic noun. This is the position of many exegetes, and it is the meaning of Muqatil's statement.

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿in the best of stature﴾ concerning it there are four opinions.

The first: in the most balanced creation.

The second: upright in stature. Both were related from Ibn ʿAbbas.

The third: in the best form. This was said by Abu al-ʿAliyah.

The fourth: in youth and strength. This was said by ʿIkrimah.

﴿Then We returned him to the lowest of the low﴾ concerning it there are two opinions.

The first: to the most decrepit age. This was related by al-ʿAwfi from Ibn ʿAbbas, and ʿIkrimah, Ibrahim, and Qatadah said likewise. al-Dahhak said: to senility after youth, and to weakness after strength. "The lowest" are the weak, the chronically ill, and the children, and the old man is lowest of all of these. al-Farra' said: He said "lowest" in the plural because "man" (al-insan) carries the sense of a plural. You say, "This is the best standing man," and you do not say "standing ones," because you mean one person; but when you do not mean one person, you mention him in the singular and in the plural. (p-173)

The second: to the Fire. This was said by al-Hasan, Abu al-ʿAliyah, and Mujahid. The meaning is: We do this to many people. The Arabs say, "So-and-so spent his wealth on so-and-so," when he only spent part of it, and similar is His statement, exalted is He: ﴿He who gives his wealth to purify himself﴾ [al-Layl: 18], not meaning all of his wealth. Then He made an exception from "man," saying: ﴿except those who believe﴾, because the sense of "man" is many.

The exegetes differ on the meaning of the exception, with two opinions.

The first: "except those who believe," for they are not returned to senility and the lowest age even if they live long. This is according to the first opinion. Ibn ʿAbbas said: whoever recites the Qur'an will not be returned to the lowest age. al-Nakhaʿi said: when a believer reaches an age in which he is unable to act, what he used to do is recorded for him, and this is His statement, exalted is He: ﴿for them is a reward never cut off﴾. Ibn Qutaybah said: the meaning is: except those who believed during the time of strength and capability, for they, in old age, are not diminished even if they are unable to perform acts of obedience, because Allah, exalted is He, knew that if He had not taken away their strength they would not have ceased from good deeds, so He continues to record for them the reward of that.

The second: "except those who believe," for they are not returned to the Fire. This is according to the second opinion.

We have already explained the meaning of "mamnun" under "Nun" [68:3].

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿So what causes you to deny the Judgment after this?﴾ concerning it there are two opinions.

(p-174) The first: "So what causes you, O man, to deny the Judgment after this proof?" That is: what is it that makes you deny the recompense? This is a rebuke to the disbeliever, and it is the meaning of Muqatil's statement. He claimed it was revealed concerning ʿAdi ibn Rabiʿah.

The second: "Who could deny you regarding reward and punishment after it has become clear to him that We created man in the way We have described?" This was said by al-Farra'. As for "the Judgment" (al-din), it is the recompense, and the reference in mentioning it is to the Resurrection, as if He were arguing from the alternation of conditions to the Resurrection.

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Is not Allah the most just of judges?﴾ That is: the most decisive of judges. Muqatil said: He judges between you and those who deny you. Some exegetes mentioned that the meaning of this verse is consolation for him regarding their rejection and his turning away from them. Then this meaning was abrogated by the verse of the sword.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: whoever recites the Qur'an will not be returned to the lowest age. al-Nakhaʿi said: when a believer reaches an age in which he is unable to act, what he used to do is recorded for him, and this is His statement, exalted is He: ﴿for them is a reward never cut off﴾. Ibn Qutaybah said: the meaning is: except those who believed during the time of strength and capability, for they, in old age, are not diminished even if they are unable to perform acts of obedience, because Allah, exalted is He, knew that if He had not taken away their strength they would not have ceased from good deeds, so He continues to record for them the reward of that.

The second: "except those who believe," for they are not returned to the Fire. This is according to the second opinion.

We have already explained the meaning of "mamnun" under "Nun" [68:3].

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿So what causes you to deny the Judgment after this?﴾ concerning it there are two opinions.

(p-174) The first: "So what causes you, O man, to deny the Judgment after this proof?" That is: what is it that makes you deny the recompense? This is a rebuke to the disbeliever, and it is the meaning of Muqatil's statement. He claimed it was revealed concerning ʿAdi ibn Rabiʿah.

The second: "Who could deny you regarding reward and punishment after it has become clear to him that We created man in the way We have described?" This was said by al-Farra'. As for "the Judgment" (al-din), it is the recompense, and the reference in mentioning it is to the Resurrection, as if He were arguing from the alternation of conditions to the Resurrection.

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Is not Allah the most just of judges?﴾ That is: the most decisive of judges. Muqatil said: He judges between you and those who deny you. Some exegetes mentioned that the meaning of this verse is consolation for him regarding their rejection and his turning away from them. Then this meaning was abrogated by the verse of the sword.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 95, verse 1–8:

(p-168) Surat al-Tin

There are two opinions concerning it:

The first: it is Meccan. This is the view of the majority, including al-Hasan and ʿAṭāʾ.

The second: it is Madani. This was related by al-Mawardi from Ibn ʿAbbas and Qatadah.

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿By the fig and the olive﴾. Concerning these two there are seven opinions.

The first: it refers to the well-known fig and the well-known olive. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Hasan, ʿAṭāʾ, Mujahid, ʿIkrimah, Jabir ibn Zayd, and Ibrahim. Some exegetes mentioned (p-169) that He swore by the fig because it is a fruit free from any impurity of distress, and this indicates the power of the One who made it upon that quality. Each single fig was made to be the size of a morsel. He swore by the olive because of the great benefit derived from it.

The second: the fig is the Mosque of Noah, peace be upon him, which was built upon al-Judi. The olive is Bayt al-Maqdis. ʿAṭiyyah related this from Ibn ʿAbbas.

The third: the fig is the Masjid al-Haram, and the olive is al-Masjid al-Aqsa. This was said by al-Dahhak.

The fourth: the fig is the Mosque of Damascus, and the olive is Bayt al-Maqdis. This was said by Kaʿb, Qatadah, and Ibn Zayd.

The fifth: they are two mountains. This was said by ʿIkrimah in one narration. It was related from Qatadah that he said: the fig is the mountain upon which Damascus stands, and the olive is the mountain upon which Bayt al-Maqdis stands.

The sixth: the fig is the Mosque of the People of the Cave, and the olive is the Mosque of Iliya. This was said by al-Qurazi.

The seventh: the fig is mountains between Hulwan and Hamadhan, and the olive is mountains in al-Sham. This was related by al-Farra'.

As for "Tur Sinin": Tur is a mountain. Concerning it there are two opinions.

(p-170) The first: it is the mountain upon which Allah spoke to Musa, peace be upon him. This was said by Kaʿb al-Ahbar, and most scholars agree.

The second: it is a mountain in al-Sham. This was said by Qatadah.

As for "Sinin": it is a dialectal form of Sina'. ʿAli, Saʿd ibn Abi Waqqas, Abu al-ʿAliyah, and Abu Mijlaz read "Wa-Tur Sina'" with a long vowel and a hamzah, with the sin vowelled with a fatha. Ibn Mas'ud, Abu al-Darda', and Abu Haywah read "Wa-Tur Sina'" like them, except that they vowelled the sin with a kasra. Abu Raja' and al-Jahdari read "Sinin" as it is in the Mushaf, but they vowelled the sin with a fatha. Ibn al-Anbari said: "Sinin" is Sina'.

They differed about its meaning. It was said: its meaning is "the good." It was said: "the blessed." It was said: it is a name for the tree around it. We have explained this in Surat al-Mu'minun [23:20]. Al-Zajjaj said: it has been read here as "Wa-Tur Sina'," and this is more fitting given His statement, exalted is He: ﴿and a tree that grows out of Mount Sinai﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 20]. Muqatil said: every mountain in which there is fruit-bearing trees is "Sinin," and Sina' is the language of the Nabat.

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿and this secure city﴾ means Makkah, where the one who fears is secure in the Jahiliyyah (p-171) and in Islam. Al-Farra' said: the meaning of "al-Amin" is "the secure," and the Arabs say of the trustworthy: "amin" (secure).

The poet said:

Do you not know, O Asma, woe to you, that I have sworn an oath not to betray my trustworthy one?

He means "amini" (my secure one).

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Certainly We created man﴾ is the answer to the oath. Concerning the intended meaning of "man" here there are five opinions.

The first: he is Kaladah ibn Usayd. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah. This was said by ʿAṭāʾ.

The third: Abu Jahl ibn Hisham.

The fourth: ʿUtbah and Shaybah; al-Mawardi related both.

(p-172) The fifth: it is a generic noun. This is the position of many exegetes, and it is the meaning of Muqatil's statement.

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿in the best of stature﴾ concerning it there are four opinions.

The first: in the most balanced creation.

The second: upright in stature. Both were related from Ibn ʿAbbas.

The third: in the best form. This was said by Abu al-ʿAliyah.

The fourth: in youth and strength. This was said by ʿIkrimah.

﴿Then We returned him to the lowest of the low﴾ concerning it there are two opinions.

The first: to the most decrepit age. This was related by al-ʿAwfi from Ibn ʿAbbas, and ʿIkrimah, Ibrahim, and Qatadah said likewise. al-Dahhak said: to senility after youth, and to weakness after strength. "The lowest" are the weak, the chronically ill, and the children, and the old man is lowest of all of these. al-Farra' said: He said "lowest" in the plural because "man" (al-insan) carries the sense of a plural. You say, "This is the best standing man," and you do not say "standing ones," because you mean one person; but when you do not mean one person, you mention him in the singular and in the plural. (p-173)

The second: to the Fire. This was said by al-Hasan, Abu al-ʿAliyah, and Mujahid. The meaning is: We do this to many people. The Arabs say, "So-and-so spent his wealth on so-and-so," when he only spent part of it, and similar is His statement, exalted is He: ﴿He who gives his wealth to purify himself﴾ [al-Layl: 18], not meaning all of his wealth. Then He made an exception from "man," saying: ﴿except those who believe﴾, because the sense of "man" is many.
